entries.0c26d05b52b7c07de43c9cdeb7ea45710c51086f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv101"/><title type="x-ms">Nahum</title> <div sID="gen20519" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">The</hi> name of this prophet signifies a <hi type="italic">comforter;</hi> for it was a charge given to all the prophets, <hi type="italic">Comfort you, comfort you, my people:</hi> and even this prophet, though wholly taken up in foretelling the destruction of Nineveh, which speaks terror to the Assyrians, is, even in that, comforter to the ten tribes of Israel, who, it is probable, were now lately carried captives into Assyria. It is very uncertain at what time he lived and prophesied, but it is most probable that he lived in the time of Hezekiah, and prophesied against Nineveh, after the captivity of Israel by the king of Assyria, which was in the ninth year of Hezekiah, and before Sennacherib's invading Judah, which was in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, for to that attempt, and the defeat of it, it is supposed, the first chapter has reference; and it is probable that it was delivered a little before it, for the encouragement of God's people in that day of treading down and perplexity. It is the conjecture of the learned Huetius that the two other chapters of this book were delivered by Nahum some years after, perhaps in the reign of Manasseh, and in that reign the Jewish chronologies generally place him, somewhat nearer to the time when Nineveh was conquered, and the Assyrian monarchy reduced, by Cyaxares and Nebuchadnezzar, some time before the first captivity of Judah. It is probable that Nahum did by word of mouth prophesy many things concerning Israel and Judah, as it is certain that Jonah did (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2 Kings xiv. 25</reference>), though we have nothing of either of them in writing, but what related to Nineveh, of which though a great and ancient city, yet probably we should never have heard in sacred writ if the Israel of God had not had some concern in it. <div eID="gen20520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20521" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20522" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The inscription of the book, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. A magnificent display of the glory of God, in a mixture of wrath and justice against the wicked, and mercy and grace towards his people, and the discovery of his majesty and power in both, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.2-Nah.1.8">ver. 2-8</reference>. III. A particular application of this (as most interpreters think) to the destruction of Sennacherib and the Assyrian army, when they besieged Jerusalem, which was a very memorable and illustrious instance of the power both of God's justice and of his mercy, and spoke abundance of terror to his enemies and encouragement to his faithful servants, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.9-Nah.1.16">ver. 9-16</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv101"/> <div eID="gen20522" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20521" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Inscription of the Book. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20523" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. <div eID="gen20523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20524" type="x-p"/> This title directs us to consider, 1. The great city against which the word of the Lord is here delivered; it is the <hi type="italic">burden of Nineveh,</hi> not only a prophecy, and a weighty one, but a burdensome prophecy, a dead weight to Nineveh, a mill-stone hanged about its neck. Nineveh was the place concerned, and the Assyrian monarchy, which that was the royal seat of. About 100 years before this Jonah had, in God's name, foretold the speedy overthrow of this great city; but then the Ninevites repented and were spared, and that decree did not <hi type="italic">bring forth.</hi> The Ninevites then saw clearly how much it was to their advantage to turn from their evil way; it was the saving of their city; and yet, soon after, they returned to it again; it became worse than ever, <hi type="italic">a bloody city,</hi> and <hi type="italic">full of lies</hi> and <hi type="italic">robbery.</hi> They repented of their repentance, returned with the dog to his vomit, and at length grew worse than ever they had been. Then God sent them not this prophet, as Jonah, but this prophecy, to read them their doom, which was now irreversible. Note, The reprieve will not be continued if the repentance be not continued in. If men turn from the good they began to do, they can expect no other than that God should turn from the favour he began to show, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.10">Jer. xviii. 10</reference>. 2. The poor prophet by whom the word of the Lord is here delivered: It is <hi type="italic">the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.</hi> The burden of Nineveh was what the prophet plainly foresaw, for it was his vision, and what he left upon record (it is the <hi type="italic">book of the vision</hi>), that, when he was gone, the event might be compared with the prediction and might confirm it. All the account we have of the prophet himself is that he was an <hi type="italic">Elkoshite,</hi> of the town called <hi type="italic">Elkes,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Elcos,</hi> which, Jerome says, was in Galilee. Some observe that the scripture ordinarily says little of the prophets themselves, that our faith might not stand upon their authority, but upon that of the blessed Spirit by whom their prophecies were indited.
entries.caa8abc4f90584caf6a01871222d5c62e50de4b3: <div eID="gen20524" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Nineveh; The Awful Power of God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20525" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> jealous, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> revengeth; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> revengeth, and <hi type="italic">is</hi> furious; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth <hi type="italic">wrath</hi> for his enemies. <hi type="super">3</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit <hi type="italic">the wicked:</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dust of his feet. <hi type="super">4</hi> He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers: Bashan languisheth, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languisheth. <hi type="super">5</hi> The mountains quake at him, and the hills melt, and the earth is burned at his presence, yea, the world, and all that dwell therein. <hi type="super">6</hi> Who can stand before his indignation? and who can abide in the fierceness of his anger? his fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by him. <hi type="super">7</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him. <hi type="super">8</hi> But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies. <div eID="gen20525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20526" type="x-p"/> Nineveh knows not God, that God that contends with her, and therefore is here told what a God he is; and it is good for us all to mix faith with that which is here said concerning him, which speaks a great deal of terror to the wicked and comfort to good people; for this glorious description of the Sovereign of the world, like the pillar of cloud and fire, has a bright side towards Israel and a dark side towards the Egyptians. Let each take his portion from it; let sinners read it and tremble; let saints read it and triumph. The wrath of God is here revealed from heaven against him enemies, his favour and mercy are here assured to his faithful loyal subjects, and his almighty power in both, making his wrath very terrible and his favour very desirable. <div eID="gen20526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20527" type="x-p"/> I. He is a God of inflexible justice, a jealous God, and will take vengeance on his enemies; let Nineveh know this, and tremble before him. Their idols are insignificant things; there is nothing formidable in them. But the God of Israel is greatly to be feared; for, 1. He resents the affronts and indignities done him by those that deny his being or any of his perfections, that set up other gods in competition with him, that destroy his laws, arraign his proceedings, ridicule his word, or are abusive to his people. Let such know that Jehovah, the one only living and true God, is a <hi type="italic">jealous God, and a revenger;</hi> he is jealous for the comfort of his worshippers, <hi type="italic">jealous for his land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.18">Joel ii. 18</reference>), and will not have that injured. He is a revenger, <hi type="italic">and he is furious;</hi> he <hi type="italic">has fury</hi> (so the word is), not as man has it, in whom it is an ungoverned passion (so he has said, <hi type="italic">Fury is not in me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Isa. xxvii. 4</reference>), but he has it in such a way as becomes the righteous God, to put an edge upon his justice, and to make it appear more terrible to those who otherwise would stand in no awe of it. He is <hi type="italic">Lord of anger</hi> (so the Hebrew phrase is for that which we read, <hi type="italic">he is furious</hi>); he has anger, but he has it at command and under government. Our anger is often lord over us, as theirs that have <hi type="italic">no rule over their own spirits,</hi> but God is always <hi type="italic">Lord of his anger</hi> and <hi type="italic">weighs a path to it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.50">Ps. lxxviii. 50</reference>. 2. He resolves to reckon with those that put those affronts upon him. We are told here, not only that he is a revenger, but that he <hi type="italic">will take vengeance;</hi> he has said he will, he has sworn it, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.40-Deut.32.41">Deut. xxxii. 40, 41</reference>. Whoever are his adversaries and enemies among men, he will make them feel his resentments; and, though the sentence against his enemies is not executed speedily, yet he reserves wrath for them and reserves them for it in the day of wrath. Against his own people, who repent and humble themselves before him, he keeps <hi type="italic">not his anger for ever,</hi> but against his enemies he will for ever let out his anger. <hi type="italic">He will not at all acquit the wicked</hi> that sin, and stand to it, and do not repent, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">v. 3</reference>. Those <hi type="italic">wickedly depart from their God</hi> that depart, and never return (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.21">Ps. xviii. 21</reference>), and these he will not acquit. Humble supplicants will find him gracious, but scornful beggars will not find him easy, or that the door of mercy will be opened to a loud, but late, Lord, Lord. This revelation of the wrath of God against his enemies is applied to Nineveh (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">v. 8</reference>), and should be applied by all those to themselves who go on still in their trespasses: <hi type="italic">With an over-running flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof.</hi> The army of the Chaldeans shall overrun the country of the Assyrians, and lay it all waste. God's judgments, when they come with commission, are like a deluge to any people, which they cannot keep off nor make head against. <hi type="italic">Darkness shall pursue his enemies;</hi> terror and trouble shall follow them, whithersoever they go, shall pursue them to utter darkness; if they think to flee from the darkness which pursues them they will but fall into that which is before them. <div eID="gen20527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20528" type="x-p"/> II. He is a God of irresistible power, and is able to deal with his enemies, be they ever so many, ever so mighty, ever so hardy. He is <hi type="italic">great in power</hi> (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">v. 3</reference>), and therefore it is good having him our friend and bad having him our enemy. Now here, <div eID="gen20528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20529" type="x-p"/> 1. The power of God is asserted and proved by divers instances of it in the kingdom of nature, where we always find its visible effects in the ordinary course of nature, and sometimes in the surprising alterations of that course. (1.) If we look up into the regions of the air, there we shall find proofs of his power, for <hi type="italic">he has his ways in the whirlwind and the storm.</hi> Which way soever God goes he carries a whirlwind and a storm along with him, for the terror of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Ps. xviii. 9</reference>, &c. And, wherever there is a whirlwind and a storm, God has the command of it, the control of it, makes his way through it, goes on his way in it, and serves his own purposes by it. He spoke to Job out of the whirlwind, and even <hi type="italic">stormy winds fulfil his word.</hi> He has <hi type="italic">his way in the whirlwind,</hi> that is, he goes on undiscerned, and the methods of his providence are to us unaccountable; as it is said, <hi type="italic">His way is in the sea. The clouds are the dust of his feet;</hi> he treads on them, walks on them, raises them when he pleases, as a man with his feet raises a cloud of dust. It is but by permission, or usurpation rather, that the devil is the prince of the power of the air, for that power is in God's hand. (2.) If we cast our eye upon the great deeps, there we find that the sea is his, for he made it; for, when he pleases, <hi type="italic">he rebukes the sea and makes it dry, by drying up all the rivers</hi> with which it is continually supplied. He gave those proofs of his power when he divided the Red Sea and Jordan, and can do the same again whenever he pleases. (3.) If we look round us on this earth, we find proofs of his power, when, either by the extreme heat and drought of summer or the cold and frost of winter, <hi type="italic">Bashan languishes, and Carmel, and the flower of Lebanon languishes,</hi> the choicest and strongest flower languishes. His power is often seen in earthquakes, which shake the mountains (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.5">v. 5</reference>), melt the hills, and melt them down, and level them with the plains. When he pleases <hi type="italic">the earth is burnt at his presence</hi> by the scorching heat of the sun, and he could burn it with fire from heaven, as he did Sodom, and at the end of time he will burn the world <hi type="italic">and all that dwell therein.</hi> The earth, and all the works that are therein, shall be burnt up. Thus <hi type="italic">great is the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">of great power.</hi> <div eID="gen20529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20530" type="x-p"/> 2. This is particularly applied to his anger. If God be an almighty God, we may thence infer (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who can stand before his indignation?</hi> The Ninevites had once found God <hi type="italic">slow to anger</hi> (as he says <reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">v. 3</reference>), and perhaps presumed upon the mercy they had then had experience of, and thought they might make bold with him; but they will find he is just and jealous as well as merciful and gracious, and, having shown the justice of his wrath, in the next he shows the power of it, and the utter insufficiency of his enemies to contend with him. It is in vain for the stoutest and strongest of sinners to think to make their part good against the power of God's anger. (1.) See God here as <hi type="italic">a consuming fire,</hi> terrible and mighty. Here is his indignation against sin, and the <hi type="italic">fierceness of his anger,</hi> his fury <hi type="italic">poured out,</hi> not like water, but <hi type="italic">like fire,</hi> like the fire and brimstone rained on Sodom, <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Ps. xi. 6</reference>. Hell is the fierceness of God's anger, <reference osisRef="Rev.16.19">Rev. xvi. 19</reference>. God's anger is so fierce that it beats down all before it: <hi type="italic">The rocks are thrown down by him,</hi> which seemed immovable. Rocks have sometimes been rent by the eruption of subterraneous fires, which is a faint resemblance of the fierceness of God's anger against sinners whose hearts are rocky, for none ever hardened their hearts against him and prospered. (2.) See sinners here are stubble before the fire, weak and impotent, and a very unequal match for the wrath of God. [1.] They are utterly unable to bear up against it, so as to resist it, and put by the strokes of it: <hi type="italic">Who can stand before his indignation?</hi> Not the proudest and most daring sinner; not the world of the ungodly; no, not the angels that sinned. [2.] They are utterly unable to bear up under it so as to keep up their spirits, and preserve any enjoyment of themselves: <hi type="italic">Who can abide in the fierceness of his anger?</hi> As it is irresistible, so it is intolerable. Some of the effects of God's displeasure in this world a man may bear up under, but the <hi type="italic">fierceness of his anger,</hi> when it fastens immediately upon the soul, who can bear? Let us therefore <hi type="italic">fear before him;</hi> let us <hi type="italic">stand in awe, and not sin.</hi> <div eID="gen20530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20531" type="x-p"/> III. He is a God of infinite mercy; and in the midst of all this wrath mercy is remembered. <hi type="italic">Let the sinners in Zion be afraid,</hi> that go on still in their transgressions, but let not those that trust in God tremble before him. For, 1. He <hi type="italic">is slow to anger</hi> (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">v. 3</reference>), not easily provoked, but ready to show mercy to those who have offended him and to receive them into favour upon their repentance. 2. When the tokens of his rage against the wicked are abroad he takes care for the safety and comfort of his own people (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is good</hi> to those that are <hi type="italic">good,</hi> and to them he will be <hi type="italic">a stronghold in the day of trouble.</hi> Note, The same almighty power that is exerted for the terror and destruction of the wicked is engaged, and shall be employed, for the protection and satisfaction of his own people; he is able both to save and to destroy. In the day of public trouble, when God's judgments are in the earth, laying all waste, he will be a place of defence to those that by faith put themselves under his protection, those that trust in him in the way of their duty, that live a life of dependence upon him, and devotedness to him; he knows them, he owns them for his, he takes cognizance of their case, knows what is best for them, and what course to take most effectually for their relief. They are perhaps obscure and little regarded in the world, but the Lord knows them, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Ps. i. 6</reference>.
entries.6419268fedb8bf40a13b0a8cdf09c03097af6d1a: <div eID="gen20531" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Destruction of the Assyrian Army; Overthrow of Sennacherib. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen20532" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> What do ye imagine against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? he will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time. <hi type="super">10</hi> For while <hi type="italic">they be</hi> folden together <hi type="italic">as</hi> thorns, and while they are drunken <hi type="italic">as</hi> drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry. <hi type="super">11</hi> There is <hi type="italic">one</hi> come out of thee, that imagineth evil against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , a wicked counsellor. <hi type="super">12</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Though <hi type="italic">they be</hi> quiet, and likewise many, yet thus shall they be cut down, when he shall pass through. Though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more. <hi type="super">13</hi> For now will I break his yoke from off thee, and will burst thy bonds in sunder. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath given a commandment concerning thee, <hi type="italic">that</hi> no more of thy name be sown: out of the house of thy gods will I cut off the graven image and the molten image: I will make thy grave; for thou art vile. <hi type="super">15</hi> Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off. <div eID="gen20532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20533" type="x-p"/> These verses seem to point at the destruction of the army of the Assyrians under Sennacherib, which may well be reckoned a part of the burden of Nineveh, the head city of the Assyrian empire, and a pledge of the destruction of Nineveh itself about 100 years after; and this was an event which Isaiah, with whom probably this prophet was contemporary, spoke much of. Now observe here, <div eID="gen20533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20534" type="x-p"/> I. The great provocation which the Assyrians gave to God, the just and jealous God, for which, though <hi type="italic">slow to anger,</hi> he would take vengeance (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is one come out of thee, that imagines evil against the Lord</hi>—Sennacherib, and his spokesman Rabshakeh. They framed an evil letter and an evil speech, not only against Hezekiah and his people, but against God himself, reflecting upon him as level with the gods of the heathen, and unable to protect his worshippers, dissuading his people from putting confidence in him, and urging them rather to put themselves under the protection of the <hi type="italic">great king, the king of Assyria.</hi> They contrived to alter the property of Jerusalem, that it should be no longer the city of the Lord, the holy city. This one, this mighty one, so he thinks himself, that comes out of Nineveh, <hi type="italic">imagining evil against the Lord,</hi> brings upon Nineveh this burden. Never was the glorious Majesty of heaven and earth more daringly, more blasphemously affronted than by Sennacherib at that time. He was <hi type="italic">a wicked counsellor</hi> who counselled them to despair of God's protection, and surrender themselves to the king of Assyria, and endeavour to put them out of conceit with Hezekiah's reformation (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.7">Isa. xxxvi. 7</reference>); with this wicked counsellor he here expostulates (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">What do you imagine against the Lord?</hi> What a foolish wicked thing it is for you to plot against God, as if you could outwit divine wisdom and overpower omnipotence itself!" Note, There is a great deal imagined against the Lord by the gates of hell, and against the interests of his kingdom in the world; but it will prove a <hi type="italic">vain thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 1, 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">He that sits in heaven laughs</hi> at the imaginations of the pretenders to politics against him, and will turn their counsels headlong. <div eID="gen20534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20535" type="x-p"/> II. The great destruction which God would bring upon them for it, not immediately upon the whole monarchy (the ruin of that was deferred till the measure of their iniquity was full), but, <div eID="gen20535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20536" type="x-p"/> 1. Upon the army; God will <hi type="italic">make an utter end</hi> of that; it shall be totally cut off and ruined at one blow; one fatal stroke of the destroying angel shall lay them dead upon the spot; <hi type="italic">affliction shall not rise up the second time,</hi> for it shall not need. With some sinners God makes a quick despatch, does their business at once. Divine vengeance goes not by one certain rule, nor in one constant track, but one way or other, by acute diseases or chronical ones, by slow deaths or lingering ones, he will <hi type="italic">make an utter end</hi> of all his enemies, who persist in their imaginations against him. We have reason to think that the Assyrian army were mostly of the same spirit, and spoke the same language, with their general, and now God would take them to task, though they did but say as they were taught; and it shall appear that they have laid themselves open to divine wrath by their own act and deed, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.10">v. 10</reference>. (1.) They are <hi type="italic">as thorns</hi> that entangle one another, and are <hi type="italic">folded together.</hi> They make one another worse, and more inveterate against God and his Israel, harden one another's hearts, and strengthen one another's hands, in their impiety; and therefore God will do with them as the husbandman does with a bush of thorns when he cannot part them: he puts them all into the fire together. (2.) They are <hi type="italic">as drunken men,</hi> intoxicated with pride and rage; and such as they shall be irrecoverably overthrown and destroyed. They shall be as drunkards, besotted to their own ruin, and shall stumble and fall, and make themselves a reproach, and be justly laughed at. (3.) They shall be <hi type="italic">devoured as stubble fully dry,</hi> which is irresistibly and irrecoverably consumed by the flame. The judgments of God are as devouring fire to those that make themselves as stubble to them. It is again threatened concerning this great army (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">v. 12</reference>) that <hi type="italic">though they be quiet and likewise many,</hi> very secure, not fearing the sallies out of the besieged upon them, because <hi type="italic">they are numerous,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">thus shall they be cut down,</hi> or certainly shall they be cut down, as grass and corn are cut down, with as little ado, when <hi type="italic">he shall pass through,</hi> even the destroying angel that is commissioned to cut them down. Note, The security of sinners, and their confidence in their own strength, are often presages of ruin approaching. <div eID="gen20536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20537" type="x-p"/> 2. Upon the king. He <hi type="italic">imagined evil against the Lord,</hi> and shall he escape? No (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord has given a commandment concerning thee;</hi> the decree has gone forth, <hi type="italic">that thy name be no more sown,</hi> that thy memory perish, that thou be no more talked of as thou hast been, and that the report of thy mighty actions be dispersed upon the wings of fame and celebrated with her trumpet." Because Sennacherib's son reigned in his stead, some make this to point at the overthrow of the Assyrian empire not long after. Note, Those that <hi type="italic">imagine evil against the Lord</hi> hasten evil upon themselves and their own families and interests, and ruin their own names by dishonouring his name. It is further threatened, (1.) That the images he worshipped should be cut off from their temple, the <hi type="italic">graven image</hi> and the <hi type="italic">molten image out of the house of his gods,</hi> which, some think, was fulfilled when Sennacherib was slain by his <hi type="italic">two sons, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god,</hi> by which barbarous parricide we may suppose the temple was looked upon as defiled, and was therefore disused, and the images were cut off from it, the worshippers of those images no longer attending there. Or it may be taken more generally to denote the utter ruin of Assyria; the army of the enemy shall lay all waste, and not spare even the images of their gods, by which God would intimate to them that one of the grounds of his controversy with them was their idolatry. (2.) That Sennacherib's grave shall be made there, some think in the house of his god; there he is slain, and there he shall be buried, for <hi type="italic">he is vile;</hi> he lies under this perpetual mark of disgrace, that he had so far lost his interest in the natural affection of his own children that two of them murdered him. Or it may be meant of the ignominious fall of the Assyrian monarchy itself, upon the ruins of which that of Babylon was raised. What a noise was made about the grave of that once formidable state, but now despicable, is largely described, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.3">Ezek. xxxi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.11">11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15">15,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.16">16</reference>. Note, Those that make themselves vile by scandalous sins God will make vile by shameful punishments. <div eID="gen20537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20538" type="x-p"/> III. The great deliverance which God would hereby work for his own people and the city that was called by his name. The ruin of the church's enemies is the salvation of the church, and a very great salvation it was that was wrought for Jerusalem by the overthrow of Sennacherib's army. <div eID="gen20538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20539" type="x-p"/> 1. The siege shall hereby be raised: "<hi type="italic">Now will I break his yoke from off thee,</hi> by which thou art kept in servitude, and <hi type="italic">will burst thy bonds asunder,</hi> by which thou seemest bound over to the Assyrian's wrath." That vast victorious army, when it forced free quarters for itself throughout all the land of Judah, and lived at discretion there, was as yokes and bonds upon them. Jerusalem, when it was besieged, was, as it were, bound and fettered by it; but, when the destroying angel had done his work, Jerusalem's bonds were burst asunder, and it was set at liberty again. This was a figure of the great salvation, by which the Jerusalem that is above is made free, is made free indeed. <div eID="gen20539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20540" type="x-p"/> 2. The enemy shall be so weakened and dispirited that they shall never make any such attempt again, and the end of this trouble shall be so well gained by the grace of God that there shall be no more occasion for such a severe correction. (1.) God will not again afflict Jerusalem; his anger is <hi type="italic">turned away,</hi> and he says, <hi type="italic">It is enough;</hi> for he has by this fright <hi type="italic">accomplished his whole work upon Mount Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa. x. 12</reference>), and therefore "<hi type="italic">though I have afflicted thee, I will afflict thee no more;</hi>" the bitter portion shall not be repeated unless there be need and the patient's case call for it; for God <hi type="italic">doth not afflict willingly.</hi> (2.) The enemy shall not dare again to attack Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">The wicked shall no more pass through thee</hi> as they have done, to lay all waste, <hi type="italic">for he is utterly cut off</hi> and disabled to do it. His army is cut off, his spirit cut off, and at length he himself is cut off. <div eID="gen20540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20541" type="x-p"/> 3. The tidings of this great deliverance shall be published and welcomed with abundance of joy throughout the kingdom, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">v. 15</reference>. While Sennacherib prevailed, and carried all before him, every day brought bad news; but now, <hi type="italic">behold, upon the mountains, the feet of him that bringeth good tidings,</hi> the <hi type="italic">feet of the evangelist;</hi> he is seen coming at a distance upon the mountains, as fast as his feet will carry him; and how pleasant a sight is it once more to see a messenger of peace, after we have received so many of Job's messengers! We find these words made use of by another prophet to illustrate the mercy of the deliverance of the people of God out of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Isa. lii. 7</reference>), not that the prophets stole the word one from another (as those did, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.30">Jer. xxiii. 30</reference>), but speaking by the same Spirit, they often used the same expressions; and it may be of good use for ministers to testify their consent to wholesome truths (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1 Tim. vi. 3</reference>) by concurring in the same forms of sound words, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.13">2 Tim. i. 13</reference>. These words are also quoted by the apostle, both from Isaiah and Nahum, and applied to the great redemption wrought out for us by our Lord Jesus, and the publishing of it to the world by the everlasting gospel, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Rom. x. 15</reference>. Christ's ministers are those messengers of good tidings, that preach <hi type="italic">peace by Jesus Christ. How beautiful are the feet</hi> of those <hi type="italic">messengers!</hi> How welcome their message to those that see their misery and danger by reason of sin! And observe, He that brings these good tidings brings with them a call to Judah to <hi type="italic">keep her solemn feasts</hi> and <hi type="italic">perform her vows.</hi> During the trouble, (1.) The ordinary feasts had been intermitted. <hi type="italic">Inter arma silent leges—The voice of law cannot be heard amidst the shouts of battle.</hi> While Jerusalem was <hi type="italic">encompassed with armies</hi> they could not go thither to worship; but now that the embargo is taken off they must return to the observance of their feasts; and the feasts of the Lord will be doubly sweet to the people of God when they have been for some time deprived of the benefit of them and God graciously restores them their opportunities again, for we are taught the worth of such mercies by the want of them. (2.) They had made vows to God, that, if he would deliver them out of this distress, they would do something extraordinary in his service, to his honour; and now that the deliverance is wrought they are called upon to perform their vows; the promise they had then made must now be made good, for <hi type="italic">better it is not to vow than to vow and not to pay.</hi> And those words, <hi type="italic">The wicked shall no more pass through thee,</hi> may be taken as a promise of the perfecting of the good work of reformation which Hezekiah had begun; the wicked shall not, as they have done, walk on every side, but they shall be cut off, and the baffling of the attempts from the wicked enemies abroad is a mercy indeed to a nation when it is accompanied with the restraint and reformation of the wicked at home, who are its more dangerous enemies.  <chapter eID="Nah.1"/> <div eID="gen20541" type="x-p"/>

entries.cf25e181eabff99f0b6dd1b70f5db4b84bbd93e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12819"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23830" type="x-p"/> Nahum means "consolation" and "vengeance"; symbolizing the "consolation" in the book for God's people, and the "vengeance" coming on their enemies. In the first chapter the two themes alternate; but as the prophet advances, vengeance on the capital of the Assyrian foe is the predominant topic. He is called "the Elkoshite" (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.1">Na 1:1</reference>), from Elkosh, or Elkesi, a village of Galilee, pointed out to Jerome [Preface in Nahum] as a place of note among the Jews, having traces of ancient buildings. The name Capernaum, that is, "village of Nahum," seems to take its name from Nahum having resided in it, though born in Elkosh in the neighborhood. There is another Elkosh east of the Tigris, and north of Mosul, believed by Jewish pilgrims to be the birthplace and burial place of the prophet. But the book of Nahum in its allusions shows a particularity of acquaintance with Palestine (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.4">Na 1:4</reference>), and only a more general knowledge as to Nineveh (Na 2:4-6; 3:2, 3).<div eID="gen23830" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23829" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23831" type="x-p"/> His graphic description of Sennacherib and his army (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.9-Nah.1.12">Na 1:9-12</reference>) makes it not unlikely that he was in or near Jerusalem at the time: hence the number of phrases corresponding to those of Isaiah (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">Na 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.23">10:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.10">Na 2:10</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.24.1">Is 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.3">21:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Na 1:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>). The prophecy in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.14">Na 1:14</reference> probably refers to the murder of Sennacherib twenty years after his return from Palestine (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.38">Is 37:38</reference>). The date of his prophecies, thus, seems to be about the former years of Hezekiah. So Jerome thinks. He plainly writes while the Assyrian power was yet unbroken (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">Na 1:12</reference>; 2:11-13 <reference osisRef="Nah.3.15-Nah.3.17">Na 3:15-17</reference>). The correspondence between the sentiments of Nahum and those of Isaiah and Hezekiah, as recorded in Second Kings and Isaiah, proves the likelihood of Nahum's prophecies belonging to the time when Sennacherib was demanding the surrender of Jerusalem, and had not yet raised the siege (compare <reference osisRef="Nah.1.2">Na 1:2</reference>, &c., with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.14">2Ki 19:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.7">Na 1:7</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.22">2Ki 18:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.19">19:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.7">2Ch 32:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.9">Na 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.22">2Ki 19:22</reference>, 27, 28; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.14">Na 1:14</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.6">2Ki 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Na 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2:1, 2</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.32">2Ki 19:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.13">Na 2:13</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.22">2Ki 19:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23">23</reference>). The historical data in the book itself are the humiliation of Israel and Judah by Assyria (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.2">Na 2:2</reference>); the invasion of Judah (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.9">Na 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>); and the conquest of No-ammon, or Thebes, in Upper Egypt (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.8-Nah.3.10">Na 3:8-10</reference>). Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser had carried away Israel. The Jews were harassed by the Syrians, and impoverished by Ahaz' payments to Tiglath-pileser (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.1-2Chr.28.27">2Ch 28:1-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.9">Is 7:9</reference>). Sargon, Shalmaneser's successor, after the reduction of Phoenicia by the latter, fearing lest Egypt should join Palestine against him, undertook an expedition to Africa (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Is 20:1-6</reference>), and took Thebes; the latter fact we know only from Nahum, but the success of the expedition in general is corroborated in <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Is 20:1-6</reference>. Sennacherib, Sargon's successor, made the last Assyrian attempt against Judea, ending in the destruction of his army in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah (713-710 B.C.). As Nahum refers to this in part prophetically, in part as matter of history (Na 1:9-13; 2:13), he must have lived about 720-714 B.C., that is, almost a hundred years before the event foretold, namely, the overthrow of Nineveh by the joint forces of Cyaxares and Nabopolassar in the reign of Chyniladanus, 625 or 603 B.C.<div eID="gen23831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23832" type="x-p"/> The prophecy is remarkable for its unity of aim. Nahum's object was to inspire his countrymen, the Jews, with the assurance that, however alarming their position might seem, exposed to the attacks of the mighty Assyrian, who had already carried away the ten tribes, yet that not only should the Assyrian (Sennacherib) fail in his attack on Jerusalem, but Nineveh, his own capital, be taken and his empire overthrown; and this, not by an arbitrary exercise of Jehovah's power, but for the iniquities of the city and its people.<div eID="gen23832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23833" type="x-p"/> His position in the canon is seventh of the minor prophets in both the Hebrew and Greek arrangement. He is seventh in point of date.<div eID="gen23833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23834" type="x-p"/> His style is clear, elegant, and forcible. Its most striking characteristic is the power of representing several phases of an idea in the briefest sentences, as in the majestic description of God in the commencement, the conquest of Nineveh, and the destruction of No-ammon [Eichorn]. De Wette calls attention to his variety of manner in presenting ideas, as marking great poetic talent. "Here there is something sonorous in his language there something murmuring; with both these alternates something that is soft, delicate, and melting, as the subject demands." Excepting two alleged Assyrian words (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Na 3:17</reference>), English Version, "crowned," or princes, and English Version, "captains," or satraps (used by <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jr 51:27</reference>), the language is pure. These two, doubtless, came to be known in Judea from the intercourse with Assyria in the eighth and seventh centuries B.C.<div eID="gen23834" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Nah.1.1-Nah.1.15">Na 1:1-15</reference>. Jehovah's Attributes as a Jealous Judge of Sin, Yet Merciful to His Trusting People, Should Inspire Them with Confidence. He Will Not Allow the Assyrians Again to Assail Them, but Will Destroy the Foe.</title> <div sID="gen23835" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12819"/><hi type="bold">1. burden of Nineveh--</hi>the prophetic doom of Nineveh. Nahum prophesied against that city a hundred fifty years after Jonah. <div eID="gen23835" type="x-p"/>
entries.06d00f70124e41a71dae4c9e94a315ee0ae950b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12820"/><div sID="gen23836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12820"/><hi type="bold">2. jealous--</hi>In this there is sternness, yet tender affection. We are jealous only of those we love: a husband, of a wife; a king, of his subjects' loyalty. God is jealous of men because He loves them. God will not bear a rival in His claims on them. His burning jealousy for His own wounded honor and their love, as much as His justice, accounts for all His fearful judgments: the flood, the destruction of Jerusalem, that of Nineveh. His jealousy will not admit of His friends being oppressed, and their enemies flourishing (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.22">1Co 16:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>). Burning zeal enters into the idea in "jealous" here (compare <reference osisRef="Num.25.11">Nu 25:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.25.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.10">1Ki 19:10</reference>).<div eID="gen23836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord revengeth ... Lord revengeth--</hi>The repetition of the incommunicable name Jehovah, and of His revenging, gives an awful solemnity to the introduction.<div eID="gen23837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">furious--</hi>literally, "a master of fury." So a master of the tongue, that is, "eloquent." "One who, if He pleases, can most readily give effect to His fury" [Grotius]. Nahum has in view the provocation to fury given to God by the Assyrians, after having carried away the ten tribes, now proceeding to invade Judea under Hezekiah.<div eID="gen23838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reserveth wrath for his enemies--</hi>reserves it against His own appointed time (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.9">2Pe 2:9</reference>). After long waiting for their repentance in vain, at length punishing them. A wrong estimate of Jehovah is formed from His suspending punishment: it is not that He is insensible or dilatory, but He reserves wrath for His own fit time. In the case of the penitent, He does not reserve or retain His anger (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.9">Psa 103:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">Jr 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>). <div eID="gen23839" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee2bd9e82f388b5d3623dfdf6018587cff10773a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12821"/><div sID="gen23840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12821"/><hi type="bold">3. slow to anger, and great in power--</hi>that is, but great in power, so as to be able in a moment, if He pleases, to destroy the wicked. His long-suffering is not from want of power to punish (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Ex 34:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen23840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not at all acquit--</hi>literally, "will not acquitting acquit," or treat as innocent.<div eID="gen23841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord hath his way in the whirlwind--</hi>From this to <reference osisRef="Nah.1.5">Na 1:5</reference>, inclusive, is a description of His power exhibited in the phenomena of nature, especially when He is wroth. His vengeance shall sweep away the Assyrian foe like a whirlwind (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.25">Pr 10:25</reference>).<div eID="gen23842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clouds are the dust of his feet--</hi>Large as they are, He treads on them, as a man would on the small dust; He is Lord of the clouds, and uses them as He pleases. <div eID="gen23843" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa99c4daf0e06f472e56570d27a69d05e8b3d385: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12822"/><div sID="gen23844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12822"/><hi type="bold">4. rebuketh the sea--</hi>as Jesus did (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.26">Mt 8:26</reference>), proving Himself God (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Is 50:2</reference>).<div eID="gen23844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bashan languisheth--</hi>through drought; ordinarily it was a region famed for its rich pasturage (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.1.10">Joe 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen23845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flower of Lebanon--</hi>its bloom; all that blooms so luxuriantly on Lebanon (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.7">Ho 14:7</reference>). As Bashan was famed for its pastures, Carmel for its corn fields and vineyards, so Lebanon for its forests (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">Is 33:9</reference>). There is nothing in the world so blooming that God cannot change it when He is wroth. <div eID="gen23846" type="x-p"/>
entries.324f9c1cf953a32b551288e01cdd90224ab46541: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12823"/><div sID="gen23847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12823"/><hi type="bold">5. earth is burned--</hi>so Grotius. Rather, "lifts itself," that is, "heaveth" [Maurer]: as the Hebrew is translated in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.9">Psa 89:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.1">Ho 13:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.21">2Sa 5:21</reference>, Margin. <div eID="gen23847" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4872c13db8a804e6ee3fc5f61f396c74bbf39c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12824"/><div sID="gen23848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12824"/><hi type="bold">6. fury is poured out like fire--</hi>like the liquid fire poured out of volcanoes in all directions (see <reference osisRef="Jer.7.20">Jr 7:20</reference>).<div eID="gen23848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rocks are thrown down--</hi>or, "are burnt asunder"; the usual effect of volcanic fire (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">Jr 51:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.56">56</reference>). As Hannibal burst asunder the Alpine rocks by fire to make a passage for his army [Grotius]. <div eID="gen23849" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa01537a33fd927edc953aa91096a42093edf8ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12825"/><div sID="gen23850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12825"/>7. Here Nahum enters on his special subject, for which the previous verses have prepared the way, namely, to assure his people of safety in Jehovah under the impending attack of Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.7">Na 1:7</reference>), and to announce the doom of Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian foe (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">Na 1:8</reference>). The contrast of <reference osisRef="Nah.1.7">Na 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference> heightens the force.<div eID="gen23850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he knoweth--</hi>recognizes as His own (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.5">Ho 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Am 3:2</reference>); and so, cares for and guards (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen23851" type="x-p"/>
entries.840efacb381ff064089c1557a3e7d21044a1c761: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12826"/><div sID="gen23852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12826"/><hi type="bold">8. with an overrunning flood--</hi>that is, with irresistible might which overruns every barrier like a flood. This image is often applied to overwhelming armies of invaders. Also of calamity in general (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.7">42:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5">90:5</reference>). There is, perhaps, a special allusion to the mode of Nineveh's capture by the Medo-Babylonian army; namely, through a flood in the river which broke down the wall twenty furlongs (see on <reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">Na 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.10">11:10</reference>, 22, 40).<div eID="gen23852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">end of the place thereof--</hi>Nineveh is personified as a queen; and "her place" of residence (the Hebrew for "thereof" is feminine) is the city itself (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.8">Na 2:8</reference>), [Maurer]. Or, He shall so utterly destroy Nineveh that its place cannot be found; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">Na 3:17</reference> confirms this (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">Psa 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.35">Da 2:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.8">Re 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.11">20:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">darkness--</hi>the severest calamities. <div eID="gen23854" type="x-p"/>
entries.b173dd2b7437f5e65e29ed4797bab9724c61a01a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12827"/><div sID="gen23855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12827"/><hi type="bold">9. What do ye imagine against the Lord?--</hi>abrupt address to the Assyrians. How mad is your attempt, O Assyrians, to resist so powerful a God! What can ye do against such an adversary, successful though ye have been against all other adversaries? Ye imagine ye have to do merely with mortals and with a weak people, and that so you will gain an easy victory; but you have to encounter God, the protector of His people. Parallel to <reference osisRef="Isa.37.23-Isa.37.29">Is 37:23-29</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>.<div eID="gen23855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he will make an utter end--</hi>The utter overthrow of Sennacherib's host, soon about to take place, is an earnest of the "utter end" of Nineveh itself.<div eID="gen23856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">affliction shall not rise up the second time--</hi>Judah's "affliction" caused by the invasion shall never rise again. So <reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">Na 1:12</reference>. But Calvin takes the "affliction" to be that of Assyria: "There will be no need of His inflicting on you a second blow: He will make an utter end of you once for all" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.12">1Sa 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8">26:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.10">2Sa 20:10</reference>). If so, this verse, in contrast to <reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">Na 1:12</reference>, will express, Affliction shall visit the Assyrian no more, in a sense very different from that in which God will afflict Judah no more. In the Assyrian's case, because the blow will be fatally final; the latter, because God will make lasting blessedness in Judah's case succeed temporary chastisement. But it seems simpler to refer "affliction" here, as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.12">Na 1:12</reference>, to Judah; indeed destruction, rather than affliction, applies to the Assyrian. <div eID="gen23857" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a8c7e4176442d390b5d5835fd5d8ce162d93595: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12828"/><div sID="gen23858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12828"/><hi type="bold">10. while they are folden together as thorns--</hi>literally, "to the same degree as thorns" (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.27">1Ch 4:27</reference>, Margin). As thorns, so folded together and entangled that they cannot be loosed asunder without trouble, are thrown by the husbandmen all in a mass into the fire, so the Assyrians shall all be given together to destruction. Compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.7">7</reference>, where also "thorns" are the image of the wicked. As this image represents the speediness of their destruction in a mass, so that of "drunkards," their rushing as it were of their own accord into it; for drunkards fall down without any one pushing them [Kimchi]. Calvin explains, Although ye be dangerous to touch as thorns (that is, full of rage and violence), yet the Lord can easily consume you. But "although" will hardly apply to the next clause. English Version and Kimchi, therefore, are to be preferred. The comparison to drunkards is appropriate. For drunkards, though exulting and bold, are weak and easily thrown down by even a finger touching them. So the insolent self-confidence of the Assyrians shall precipitate their overthrow by God. The Hebrew is "soaked," or "drunken as with their own wine." Their drunken revelries are perhaps alluded to, during which the foe (according to Diodorus Siculus [2]) broke into their city, and Sardanapalus burned his palace; though the main and ultimate destruction of Nineveh referred to by Nahum was long subsequent to that under Sardanapalus. <div eID="gen23858" type="x-p"/>
entries.a463f76022b3f5a2ef83971d9c793da626ed0644: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12829"/><div sID="gen23859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12829"/>11. The cause of Nineveh's overthrow: Sennacherib's plots against Judah.<div eID="gen23859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come out of thee--</hi>O Nineveh. From thyself shall arise the source of thy own ruin. Thou shalt have only thyself to blame for it.<div eID="gen23860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">imagineth evil--</hi>Sennacherib carried out the imaginations of his countrymen (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.9">Na 1:9</reference>) against the Lord and His people (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.22">2Ki 19:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen23861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a wicked counsellor--</hi>literally, "a counsellor of Belial." Belial means "without profit," worthless, and so bad (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.25">1Sa 25:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">2Co 6:15</reference>). <div eID="gen23862" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d985fd6dbb3a576bdfccfba7e963093773fc846: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12830"/><div sID="gen23863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12830"/>12-14. The same truths repeated as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.9-Nah.1.11">Na 1:9-11</reference>, Jehovah here being the speaker. He addresses Judah, prophesying good to it, and evil to the Assyrian.<div eID="gen23863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Though they be quiet--</hi>that is, without fear, and tranquilly secure. So Chaldee and Calvin. Or, "entire," "complete"; "Though their power be unbroken [Maurer], and though they be so many, yet even so they shall be cut down" (literally, "shorn"; as hair shaved off closely by a razor, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.20">Is 7:20</reference>). As the Assyrian was a razor shaving others, so shall he be shaven himself. Retribution in kind. In the height of their pride and power, they shall be clean cut off. The same Hebrew stands for "likewise" and "yet thus." So many as they are, so many shall they perish.<div eID="gen23864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when he shall pass through--</hi>or, "and he shall pass away," namely, "the wicked counsellor" (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.11">Na 1:11</reference>), Sennacherib. The change of number to the singular distinguishes him from his host. They shall be cut down, he shall pass away home (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.36">36</reference>) [Henderson]. English Version is better, "they shall be cut down, "when" He (Jehovah) shall pass through," destroying by one stroke the Assyrian host. This gives the reason why they with all their numbers and power are to be so utterly cut off. Compare "pass through," that is, in destroying power (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.12">Eze 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.10">Da 11:10</reference>).<div eID="gen23865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Though I have afflicted thee--</hi>Judah, "I will afflict thee no more" (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Is 40:1</reference>, 2; 52:1, 2). The contrast is between "they," the Assyrians, and "thee," Judah. Their punishment is fatal and final. Judah's was temporary and corrective. <div eID="gen23866" type="x-p"/>
entries.c240187310d1a4f7bbf3fbc5c81694a3ffb88eed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12833"/><div sID="gen23873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12833"/>15. This verse is joined in the Hebrew text to the second chapter. It is nearly the same as <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>, referring to the similar deliverance from Babylon.<div eID="gen23873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him that bringeth good tidings--</hi>announcing the overthrow of Sennacherib and deliverance of Jerusalem. The "mountains" are those round Jerusalem, on which Sennacherib's host had so lately encamped, preventing Judah from keeping her "feasts," but on which messengers now speed to Jerusalem, publishing his overthrow with a loud voice where lately they durst not have opened their mouths. A type of the far more glorious spiritual deliverance of God's people from Satan by Messiah, heralded by ministers of the Gospel (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Ro 10:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perform thy vows--</hi>which thou didst promise if God would deliver thee from the Assyrian.<div eID="gen23875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wicked--</hi>literally, "Belial"; the same as the "counsellor of Belial" (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.11">Na 1:11</reference>, Margin); namely, Sennacherib. <chapter eID="Nah.1"/>

entries.cab3be972cd49312603f0791b47ea1b8d07798d5: <div eID="gen34946" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Book of the Prophet Nahum</title> <div sID="gen34947" type="x-p"/> Nahum, the seventh of the twelve minor prophets, was a native of Elkoshai, a little village of Galilee, whose ruins were still in being in the time of St. Jerome. However there are some who think that Elkoshai is rather the name of his father, and that the place of his birth was Bethabor, or Bethabara, beyond Jordan They used to show the tomb of the prophet at a village called Beth-gabre, now called Gibbin, near Emmaus. The Chaldee calls him Nahum of Beth-koshi, or of Beth-kitsi; but the situation of this place is as much unknown as that of Elkoshai. <div eID="gen34947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34948" type="x-p"/> The particular circumstances of the life of Nahum are altogether unknown. His prophecy consists of three chapters, which make up but one discourse, wherein he foretells the destruction of Nineveh. He describes it in so lovely and pathetic a manner, that he seems to have been upon the spot to declare to the Ninevites the destruction of their city. <div eID="gen34948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34949" type="x-p"/> Opinions are divided as to the time in which he prophesied. Josephus will have it that he foretold the fall of Nineveh one hundred and fifteen years before it happened, which will bring the time of Nahum to that of King Ahaz. The Jews say that he prophesied under Manasseh. We are inclined to be of St. Jerome's opinion, that he foretold the destruction of Nineveh in the time of Hezekiah, and after the war of Sennacherib in Egypt, mentioned by Berosus. Nahum speaks plainly of the taking of No-Ammon, a city of Egypt; of the haughtiness of Rabshakeh; of the defeat of Sennacherib; and he speaks of them as things that were past. He supposes that the Jews were still in their own country, and that they there celebrated their festivals. He speaks of the captivity, and of the dispersion of the ten tribes. All these evidences convince us that Nahum cannot be placed before the fifteenth year of Hezekiah, since the expedition of Sennacherib against this prince was in the fourteenth year of his reign. <div eID="gen34949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34950" type="x-p"/> This prophet gives us a fine description of the destruction of Nineveh. He says that this city should be ruined by a deluge of waters, which should overflow it and demolish its walls. <div eID="gen34950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34951" type="x-p"/> Diodorus Siculus and Athenaeus relate, that during the time this city was besieged by Belesis and by Arbaces, under Sardanapalus, the river Tigris swelled so as to overthrow twenty furlongs of the walls of Nineveh. But as the siege mentioned by Nahum was long after the taking of Nineveh under Sardanapalus, it must needs be that the same thing happened to Nineveh at the second and last siege, under Nebuchadnezzar and Astyages. Probably the besiegers at this second siege determined the course of the waters, and brought on the same fate to the city by the same means as at the first siege. And as the walls of those ancient cities were generally formed of brick kneaded with straw and baked in the sun, a flood of waters could easily effect their dissolution. Babylon was built in the same manner; and this is the reason why scarcely any vestiges of those cities are to be found. See on <reference osisRef="Nah.3.14">Nah 3:14</reference> (note). <div eID="gen34951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34952" type="x-p"/> The time of the prophet's death is not known. The Greek meneologies and the Latin martyrologies place his festival on the first of December. Petrus Natalis places it on the twenty-fourth of the same month, which he says was the day of his death, without acquainting us whence he had learned this circumstance. <div eID="gen34952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34953" type="x-p"/> The conduct and imagery of this prophetical poem are truly admirable. <div eID="gen34953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34954" type="x-p"/> The exordium sets forth with grandeur the justice and power of God, tempered by lenity and goodness, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.1-Nah.1.8">Nah 1:1-8</reference>. <div eID="gen34954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34955" type="x-p"/> A sudden address to the Assyrians follows; and a prediction of their perplexity and overthrow, as devisers of evil against the true God, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.9-Nah.1.11">Nah 1:9-11</reference>. Jehovah himself then proclaims freedom to his people from the Assyrian yoke, and the destruction of the Assyrian idols, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.12-Nah.1.14">Nah 1:12-14</reference>. Upon which the prophet, in a most lively manner, turns the attention of Judah to the approach of the messenger who brings such glad tidings, and bids her celebrate her festivals and offer her thank-offerings, without fear of so powerful an adversary, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Nah 1:15</reference>. <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1-Nah.2.13">Nah 2:1-13</reference>. In the next place Nineveh is called on to prepare for the approach of her enemies, as instruments in the hands of Jehovah; and the military array and muster of the Medes and Babylonians, their rapid approach to the city, the process of the siege, the capture of the place, the captivity, lamentation, and flight of the inhabitants, the sacking of the wealthy city, and the consequent desolation and terror, are described in the true spirit of Eastern poetry, and with many pathetic, vivid, and sublime images, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1-Nah.2.10">Nah 2:1-10</reference>. <div eID="gen34955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34956" type="x-p"/> A grand and animated allegory succeeds this description, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.11">Nah 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.12">Nah 2:12</reference>; which is explained and applied to the city of Nineveh in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.13">Nah 2:13</reference>. <div eID="gen34956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34957" type="x-p"/> Chap. 3. The prophet denounces a wo against Nineveh for her perfidy and violence, and strongly places before our eyes the number of her chariots and cavalry, her burnished arms, and the great and unrelenting slaughter which she spread around her, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.1-Nah.3.3">Nah 3:1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen34957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34958" type="x-p"/> He assigns her idolatries as one cause of her ignominious and unpitied fall, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.4-Nah.3.7">Nah 3:4-7</reference>. <div eID="gen34958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34959" type="x-p"/> He foretells that No-Ammon, (the Diospolis in the Delta), her rival in populousness, confederacies, and situation, should share a like fate with herself, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.8-Nah.3.11">Nah 3:8-11</reference>; and beautifully illustrates the ease with which her strong holds should be taken, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.12">Nah 3:12</reference>, and her pusillanimity during the siege, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.13">Nah 3:13</reference>. <div eID="gen34959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34960" type="x-p"/> He pronounces that all her preparations, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.14">Nah 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.15">Nah 3:15</reference>, her numbers, her opulence, her multitude of chief men, would be of no avail, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.15-Nah.3.17">Nah 3:15-17</reference>. <div eID="gen34960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34961" type="x-p"/> He foretells that her tributaries would desert her, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Nah 3:18</reference>. <div eID="gen34961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34962" type="x-p"/> He concludes with a proper epiphonema; the topics of which are, the greatness and incurableness of her wound, and the just triumph of others over her on account of her extensive oppressions, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.19">Nah 3:19</reference>. <div eID="gen34962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34963" type="x-p"/> To sum up all with the decisive judgment of an eminent critic: "Not one of the minor prophets equals the sublimity, genius, and spirit of Nahum. Besides, his prophecy is a perfect poem. The exordium is exceedingly majestic. The apparatus for the destruction of Nineveh, and the description of that catastrophe, are painted in the most glowing colours, and are admirably clear and powerful." Lowth, Praelect. Hebrews 21, p. 282. <div eID="gen34963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34964" type="x-p"/> It must be farther observed, that this prophecy was highly interesting to the Jews; as the Assyrians had often ravaged their country, and I suppose had recently destroyed the kingdom of Israel. See Calmet. <div eID="gen34964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34965" type="x-p"/> This chapter opens the prophecy against the Assyrians and their metropolis with a very magnificent description of the infinite justice, tender compassion, and uncontrollable power of God, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.1-Nah.1.8">Nah 1:1-8</reference>. To this succeeds an address to the Assyrians; with a lively picture of their sudden overthrow, because of their evil device against Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.9-Nah.1.11">Nah 1:9-11</reference>. Then appears Jehovah himself, proclaiming deliverance to his people from the Assyrian yoke, and the destruction of the Assyrian idols, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.12-Nah.1.14">Nah 1:12-14</reference>; upon which the prophet, with great emphasis, directs the attention of Judah to the approach of the messenger who brings such glad tidings; and exultingly bids his people to celebrate their solemn feasts, and perform their vows, as a merciful Providence would not suffer these enemies of the Jewish state to prevail against them, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Nah 1:15</reference>. <div eID="gen34965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34966" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34967" type="x-p"/> The burden of Nineveh - משא massa not only signifies a burden, but also a thing lifted up, pronounced, or proclaimed; also a message. It is used by the prophets to signify the revelation which they have received from God to deliver to any particular people: the oracle - the prophecy. Here it signifies the declaration from God relative to the overthrow of Nineveh, and the commission of the prophet to deliver it. <div eID="gen34967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34968" type="x-p"/> As the Assyrians under Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmaneser, three of their kinds, had been employed by a just God for the chastisement of his disobedient people; the end being now accomplished by them, God is about to burn the rod wherewith he corrected Israel; and Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian empire, is to be destroyed. This prediction appears to have been accomplished a short time after this by Nebuchadnezzar and Cyaxares, the Ahasuerus of Scripture. <div eID="gen34968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34969" type="x-p"/> Nahum, נחום Nachum, signifies comforter. The name was very suitable, as he was sent to comfort the people, by showing them that God was about to destroy their adversaries.
entries.b5582b2986ef4fad7acf3194063b584a80db0780: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34970" type="x-p"/> God is jealous - For his own glory. <div eID="gen34970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34971" type="x-p"/> And - revengeth - His justice; by the destruction of his enemies. <div eID="gen34971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34972" type="x-p"/> And is furious - So powerful in the manifestations of his judgments, that nothing can stand before him. <div eID="gen34972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34973" type="x-p"/> He reserveth wrath - Though they seem to prosper for a time, and God appears to have passed by their crimes without notice, yet he reserveth - treasureth up - wrath for them, which shall burst forth in due time.
entries.83470a0337d9134eb8117e759b62d4e93df76a49: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34974" type="x-p"/> The Lord is slow to anger - He exercises much longsuffering towards his enemies, that this may lead them to repentance. And it is because of this longsuffering that vengeance is not speedily executed on every evil work. <div eID="gen34974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34975" type="x-p"/> Great in power - Able at all times to save or to destroy. <div eID="gen34975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34976" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm - These are the effects of his power; and when they appear unusual, they may be considered as the immediate effects of his power: and although he be in them to punish and destroy, he is in them to direct their course, to determine their operations, and to defend his followers from being injured by their violence. The pestilential wind which slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians did not injure one Israelite. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Kgs 19:35</reference>. <div eID="gen34976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34977" type="x-p"/> The clouds are the dust of his feet - This is spoken in allusion to a chariot and horses going on with extreme rapidity: they are all enveloped in a cloud of dust. So Jehovah is represented as coming through the circuit of the heavens as rapidly as lightning; the clouds surrounding him as the dust does the chariot and horses.
entries.5b1e61d10cae8f125cd3afcff33ee0b7285fce04: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34978" type="x-p"/> He rebuketh the sea - The Red Sea and the rivers: probably an allusion to the passage of the Red Sea and Jordan. <div eID="gen34978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34979" type="x-p"/> The description of the coming of Jehovah, from the third to the sixth verse, is dreadfully majestic. He is represented as controlling universal nature. The sea and the rivers are dried up, the mountains tremble, the hills melt, and the earth is burnt at his presence. Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon are withered and languish: streams of fire are poured out, and the rocks are cast down to make him a passage. If then, the seas, the rivers, the mountains, the hills, the rocks, and the earth itself, fail before Jehovah, or flee from his presence, how shall Nineveh and the Assyrian empire stand before him?
entries.08b8263ba8938338804e6723b609d0d42abe1ba5: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34980" type="x-p"/> The Lord is good - In the midst of judgment he remembers mercy; and among the most dreadful denunciations of wrath he mingles promises of mercy. None that trust in him need be alarmed at these dreadful threatenings; they shall be discriminated in the day of wrath, for the Lord knoweth them that trust in him.
entries.922fbcd40a9139dde4d3c6eaebdb5111aeb1e371: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34981" type="x-p"/> But with an overrunning flood - Bishop Newcome thinks this may refer to the manner in which Nineveh was taken. The Euphrates overflowed its banks, deluged a part of the city, and overturned twenty stadia of the wall; in consequence of which the desponding king burnt himself, and his palace, with his treasures. - Diodor. Sic., Edit. Wessel., p. 140, lib. ii., s. 27. <div eID="gen34981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34982" type="x-p"/> Darkness shall pursue - Calamity. All kinds of calamity shall pursue them till they are destroyed.
entries.166795018689c0d02cf9546be031feea86ef50f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34983" type="x-p"/> Affliction shall not rise up the second time - There shall be no need to repeat the judgment; with one blow God will make a full end of the business.
entries.d3a97384cfaab16383b098ab49015357431b2225: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34984" type="x-p"/> While they be folden together - However united their counsels may be, they shall be as drunken men - perplexed and unsteady in all their resolutions; and before God's judgments they shall be as dry thorns before a devouring fire.
entries.e00e3c34c7a7dd691f0038802c0d1466af11af02: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34985" type="x-p"/> Imagineth evil against the Lord - Such were Pul, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.10">2Kgs 15:10</reference>, Tiglath-pileser, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Kgs 15:29</reference>; Shalmaneser, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Kgs 17:6</reference>; and Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.17">2Kgs 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.23">2Kgs 19:23</reference>. <div eID="gen34985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34986" type="x-p"/> A wicked counsellor - Sennacherib and Rabshakeh.
entries.b87681536ab8b4f3daeabf07cb3c264b600c126b: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34987" type="x-p"/> Though they be - many - Sennacherib invaded Judea with an army of nearly two hundred thousand men. <div eID="gen34987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34988" type="x-p"/> Thus shall they be cut down - The angel of the Lord (a suffocating wind) slew of them in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Kgs 19:35</reference>.
entries.7bee7bddfdebbcbf4481c2ebbfa98de1d1d6e89b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34989" type="x-p"/> Now will I break his yoke from off thee - This refers to the tribute which the Jews were obliged to pay to the Assyrians, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.14">2Kgs 17:14</reference>.
entries.25b3ff91d66e6e25695a0a624be9621822893752: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen34989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34990" type="x-p"/> No more of thy name be sown - No more of you shall be carried away into captivity. <div eID="gen34990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34991" type="x-p"/> I will make thy grave; for thou art vile - I think this is an address to the Assyrians, and especially to Sennacherib. The text is no obscure intimation of the fact. The house of his gods is to be his grave: and we know that while he was worshipping in the house of his god Nisroch, his two sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, smote him there that he died, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.37">2Kgs 19:37</reference>.
